    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

    The highlights this week: India quietly steps up mediation efforts in the Ukraine war, ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requests a upcoming passport as she signals a return home, and the United States nominates an ambassador to Pakistan after a nearly two-year vacancy.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

    The highlights this week: India quietly steps up mediation efforts in the Ukraine war, ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requests a new passport as she signals a return home, and the United States nominates an ambassador to Pakistan after a nearly two-year vacancy.

    As Russian, Ukrainian, and U.S. officials met in Abu Dhabi for three-way talks this week, India has quietly stepped up its own mediation efforts in the Ukraine war.

    In a recent development, on Tuesday, Randhir Jaiswal, a spokesperson for India’s Ministry of External Affairs, stated New Delhi was talking with Kyiv and Moscow “at the highest level.” His comments came a day after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.

    According to recent reports, the Indian interventions reportedly focus on easing the economic consequences of the war, pushing for safer commercial shipping in the Black Sea and addressing concerns about energy and grain exports. Upcoming Delhi is also involved in conversations about how to end the conflict. Last month, an Indian truce proposal was well received by both Kyiv and Moscow, the Hindustan Times reports.

    India is a logical Russia-Ukraine mediator. It has a deep, long-standing partnership with Moscow and friendly relations with Kyiv. It also has solid ties with other key third-party actors, such as the European Union and the Arab states; its relations with Washington—despite tensions during in President Donald Trump’s second term—remain workable.

    It has been revealed that further, India has a strong interest in the war coming to an end. A longer conflict could wear down Russia’s capacity to export oil and weapons to India. It could also increase Moscow’s dependence on Beijing, a strategic competitor of New Delhi. The conflict also creates headaches for Indian foreign policy, complicating efforts to balance ties with Russia and the West.

    But India’s special relationship with Russia is a potential asset for peace, giving Newly introduced Delhi the diplomatic space to make tough demands of Moscow. Modi has repeatedly called for an end to the war—a message he delivered while sitting next to Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2022. Few non-Western leaders have pushed for peace more than Modi and certainly not as publicly.

    There were reasons to believe that India would hold back from mediating in the Ukraine war. The country rejects the role of intermediaries in its own conflicts, including its dispute with Pakistan over Kashmir. But Modi has noted he is prepared to help facilitate an end to the conflict, with pledges to Zelensky in Kyiv and during a visit to Warsaw, Poland, in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that there were also reasons to believe that India wouldn’t want to insert itself into complicated diplomatic efforts involving the United States and the EU and that it would only mediate if asked by the two belligerents. However, recent days suggest that Russia and Ukraine are both on board with such a role for India.

    Zelensky has sought Indian assistance in ending the war, according to Ukrainian media. And Russian state media have reported that Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reacted to Fresh Delhi’s proposed truce by saying, “We are grateful to our Indian friends for such readiness and the ideas that are being offered.” Putin has stated Modi has “very good ideas” for ending the war.

    To be sure, India will struggle to succeed, with fighting in Ukraine intensifying in recent days. And it likely won’t want to upstage the United States, which clearly wants to be the prime mediator—even though its tense relations with Russia make that difficult.

    But this may present an opportunity for India. With Trump perhaps wanting to be remembered as a peacemaker, the United States will likely ramp up its efforts. New Delhi—arguably the best-positioned third party—could coordinate its work with Washington, pursuing specific objectives tied to shipping and export concerns as the Trump administration focuses on broader goals.

    Such collaborations could help advance peace efforts—and deliver a boost to U.S.-India ties in the process.

    It has been revealed that ousted Hasina requests new passport. Former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has been living in India since she was ousted amid mass protests in 2024, has requested a new passport from the Bangladesh High Commission in London, via her lawyers. The move is the latest indication that Hasina wants to return to Bangladesh this year.

    During Hasina’s final days in power, security forces cracked down hard on protesters. As many as 1,400 people were killed. Hasina fled to India and last year was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity.

    In July, Hasina unveiled intends to return home and present herself in court. The government promptly rejected her request. Bangladeshi State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said the country would not give a “passport to a terrorist,” citing Bangladesh’s extradition treaty with India and demanding that Hasina be handed over.

    In a recent development, hasina’s passport request comes amid skepticism that she will follow through. Her arrest is almost guaranteed; this week, the prosecutor who secured Hasina’s death sentence warned that if she returned, she would face execution. Hasina’s vow to return might be an attempt to energize her struggling party. But without a passport, she might not be able to enter the country.

    Recent findings suggest that U.S. nominates ambassador to Pakistan. The Trump administration has nominated Natalie Baker, the U.S. chargé d’affaires in Islamabad, to be the next U.S. ambassador to Pakistan. She would succeed Donald Blome, who left the job in January 2025. Baker has been at the embassy since August 2024, when she arrived as deputy chief of mission.

    The nomination will go down well in Islamabad, where Baker is popular. She has robustly pursued what the Trump administration describes as “commercial diplomacy.” For example, Baker has driven efforts to encourage U.S. businesses to invest in Pakistan’s critical minerals. (Islamabad hosts a major forum on critical minerals this week.).

    Baker has also attracted positive attention for her public diplomacy, with many appearances at cultural events around the country.

    Sonia Gandhi’s memoir makes waves. Sonia Gandhi, the Italian-born former leader of the opposition Indian National Congress party, released a much-anticipated memoir this week. She is one of India’s biggest names; the Gandhi family dominated politics for decades until Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) took office in 2014.

    Belonging: A Journey of Love provides a rare window into Gandhi’s life. Her personal history is rich and tragic. Born in 1946, she had a modest upbringing in Italy, meeting her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, in Cambridge, England. She ended up atop the Gandhi family dynasty after the assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, and Rajiv Gandhi in 1984 and 1991, respectively.

    Though Gandhi insists that the memoir is personal, not political, the BJP has criticized it. Party spokesperson C.R. Kesavan mentioned it amounts to a “whitewashing” of the Congress party’s actions, including controversial moments under the premiership of Indira Gandhi: the 1975-77 state of Emergency and the deadly siege of a revered Sikh temple that prompted her assassination.

    The book also comes at a difficult moment for the BJP, which is grappling with large protests mounted by government critics, including the Congress party.

    Recent findings suggest that pakistanis, along with many people in the Muslim world, celebrated the victory of Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed in last week’s U.S. midterm elections. El-Sayed will be the first Muslim U.S. senator. But in Pakistan, those celebrations might be dampened by comments that he made on ABC News soon after the election.

    According to recent reports, el-Sayed slammed Pakistan, arguing that the United States shouldn’t provide assistance to countries that use it to violate international law. He identified Pakistan as one of those countries, along with Egypt, Israel, and Jordan.

    Progressive Democrats are often tough on other countries (along with their own) when it comes to human rights and democracy, so El-Sayed’s critique of Pakistan—which has seen high levels of repression in recent months—is unsurprising. More significantly, his comments might preview the challenges that a Democratic Congress could pose to Pakistani authorities.

    According to recent reports, though the U.S.-Pakistan relationship is unlikely to be affected while Trump is still in power, Islamabad may need to deal with some reputational risks. The upcoming Congress may convene hearings on Pakistan’s internal situation and might be more receptive to Pakistani American advocacy critical of the government in Islamabad.

    Sources indicate that pakistani Americans have pressed U.S. legislators to condemn Pakistan’s human rights situation and to call for the release of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan.

    #6802. Donald Trump is now radioactive

    Donald Trump is now radioactive

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pretend I’m on the ballot, the president of the United States repeatedly told American voters over the last several weeks.
    • The astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump.
    • Many larger political questions will emerge from this epic defeat, which will see any and all surviving elected Republicans (not that there are many) scurrying for cover and trying to establish as much distance as possible from Trump.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pretend I’m on the ballot, the president of the United States repeatedly told American voters over the last several weeks. Millions of voters did exactly that. Be careful what you wish for, my dude.

    The astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump. Those neutral-sounding terms of art are not remotely adequate. This was a historic smackdown, a massive, crushing defeat on a scale suffered by no incumbent president in living memory. It represents this nation’s collective awakening — admittedly rather late in the game — to this individual’s uniquely poisonous effects on our public life and civil society.

    Many larger political questions will emerge from this epic defeat, which will see any and all surviving elected Republicans (not that there are many) scurrying for cover and trying to establish as much distance as possible from Trump. They will lose his number. They will profess that they were never convinced MAGA believers, or that they secretly disagreed with the ICE reign of terror, with the war in Iran, with the disastrous tariffs, with the ideological assault on liberal democracy.

    Is JD Vance still a plausible 2028 presidential contender, having hitched his wagon to this tyrant, who has now been thoroughly pantsed in public and exposed as a pathetic loser? Will Pete Hegseth get even one more opportunity for podcaster-style flexing before the defanged Pentagon press corps? Let’s give Marco Rubio an infinitesimal amount of credit for creeping quietly through the corridors of power and staying out of the headlines. Whether his neocon mouse act is enough to survive the Trumpocalypse moment remains to be seen.

    According to recent reports, in his inimitable style, Trump is already blaming others for this defeat. He has accused Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — who lost his seat to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in one of Tuesday night’s numerous shockers — of being a RINO sellout. As impossible as it is to talk about honor with these people, that is an act of dishonorable treachery, given how eagerly Abbott has crawled and begged and prostrated himself before the Trumpian throne.

    Then again, in an ass-backward way, Trump has a point. He didn’t do this all by himself; no one could have managed that. He loaded up the pipe with bigotry and xenophobia and fear and insane conspiracy theories, and adult Republican humans who used to believe in wrong-headed but somewhat sane political doctrines inhaled it all eagerly, persuading themselves that the resulting high would insulate them from the failure of their ideas. It only made the problem worse — all the problems, really — and they should have seen that coming.

    In a recent development, the president corrupted and enslaved a historic American political party with a complicated but illustrious history, the party of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant and Dwight Eisenhower and Ronald Reagan. I’m not the biggest fan of that party either, but it has certainly had its moments, including the first woman to serve in both houses of Congress and the first Black man elected to the U.S. Senate. Trump insisted that it surrender everything to him — its principles, its history and its soul, if political parties have such a thing — and as in every fable about making a deal with the devil, now it has been destroyed.

    We don’t know how this election would have turned out in the unimaginable alternate universe where Trump stayed out of it. But he didn’t. He forced Sen. John Cornyn out of the race in Texas, in favor of Ken Paxton. Look what happened. He picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina. Look what happened. He picked Mike Collins to run against Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, and Michael Whatley to run against former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina. Look what happened. He praised Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear end and embraced gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s noxious campaign ad. Look what happened there, too.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Industry observers note that and that’s without considering the supposedly ingenious MAGA strategy of redistricting congressional seats in one state after another, with the objective of locking in a permanent Republican majority. How will that play out over the longer term? That’s impossible to say, but in 2026 it seems to have unleashed an extraordinary backlash. Forget all the hand-wringing about purple districts and swing districts; the congressional map is a nationwide wipeout. As I write this, the New York Times is predicting a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives of 256 seats. That may or may not hold up, but however this ends, it’s likely to be the biggest midterm swing in more than 30 years.

    Are there still die-hard MAGA Republicans in deep-red exurbs or rural districts who will continue to profess fealty to Trump in the wake of this catastrophe, and perhaps even maintain that it’s all some kind of grand misunderstanding? Yeah, sure. Any cult movement has its true believers and willing sacrifices. Years after his resignation, the postmistress in the rural town where I spent summers as a kid never took down the portrait of Richard Nixon. Then she retired and moved away, someone else took the job and Nixon’s picture wound up out back, in the dumpster.

    According to recent reports, that’s about where we are. Trump has always been poisonous. Republicans are finally learning that the hard way.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, sen. Susan Collins, the five-term Republican from Maine, called her opponent Troy Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, to concede Tuesday night. The Associated Press called the election just after midnight, with Jackson leading by about six percentage points.

    Despite nearly 30 years in the Senate, Collins has been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents, a smaller pebble in the blue avalanche that wiped out MAGA candidates in the midterm elections. She was the lone Senate Republican to represent a state that former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. She lost despite her efforts to distance herself from President Donald Trump. Her campaign claims she has never voted for the president and reportedly refused his help with her run.

    In a recent development, that hasn’t stopped her from often playing a key role in Trump’s agenda, casting a critical vote in Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court. Kavanaugh would later join the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to an abortion. Indeed, Collins’ position on reproductive rights seems to have played a key role in her defeat. Collins received support from Trump despite her efforts, according to reporting from ProPublica earlier this year, which revealed how an FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating Collins before Trump killed the case.

    According to recent reports, as for Jackson, he first ran for office in 2000 as a Republican for the Maine House of Representatives, but lost. He ran again as an independent two years later and won, becoming the first non-Democrat to represent the area since the late ‘70s.

    Before delegates at a state convention chose Jackson in July, Collins was originally running against oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary with support from progressive leaders. But controversies surrounding Platner continued to pile up, and he finally withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault allegations.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Recent findings suggest that through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time.
    • Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    In a recent development, A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

    Recent findings suggest that through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

    Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    #6797. Industry News: Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1083 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was originally published on The Conversation.
    • In a recent development, against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth unveiled on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone.
    • The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was originally published on The Conversation.

    In a recent development, against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth unveiled on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later said, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”.

    The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.

    For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

    Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

    And that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

    For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

    But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

    According to recent reports, as Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

    As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

    Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”.

    In a recent development, and then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

    Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

    Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”.

    Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the upcoming Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

    On the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

    Trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

    The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

    It is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

    It has been revealed that is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

    Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

    Likewise, the DHS unveiled that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

    It has been revealed that the deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia highlights – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

    Matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at more hoax bomb threats across Europe, the status of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Spain’s housing affordability crisis.

    False bomb threats once again disrupted thousands of Europeans on Wednesday in what officials and experts suspect may be part of an ongoing campaign of hybrid warfare against the continent. But rather than affecting airline passengers, this time, the threats targeted students.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at more hoax bomb threats across Europe, the status of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Spain’s housing affordability crisis.

    It has been revealed that false bomb threats once again disrupted thousands of Europeans on Wednesday in what officials and experts suspect may be part of an ongoing campaign of hybrid warfare against the continent. But rather than affecting airline passengers, this time, the threats targeted students.

    Recent findings suggest that around 6,300 schools across Italy received anonymous bomb threats on Wednesday, forcing hundreds of institutions to evacuate their classrooms. Schools in Scotland, Ireland, and Northern Ireland also received such warnings, though those emails were promptly classified as hoaxes and therefore did not disrupt learning.

    Industry observers note that the incident prompted Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to convene an emergency cabinet meeting on Wednesday with cybersecurity experts to discuss next steps. “The reports appear to be part of a strategy aimed at causing alarm and concern, which is presently being investigated in depth,” Meloni posted on social media, adding that there is no evidence to suggest that the threats pose a concrete danger.

    It is unclear who was responsible for Wednesday’s scare, though at least one email to an Italian school was reportedly signed by a “Mikhail Andropov,” the same purported author of last week’s bomb threats against newsrooms in Bulgaria and Ireland.

    At least 21 European nations have experienced similar hoaxes or actual cyberattacks in the past few weeks. That includes false bomb threats on at least 27 different European airlines, hacking operations on supermarket refrigeration systems, and coordinated cyberattacks on blood banks. These incidents have disrupted air traffic for thousands of travelers, spoiled food, sparked fires, and threatened critical healthcare infrastructure.

    “We obviously need to be vigilant,” Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara told local media on Wednesday. “But we must also be aware that in a context where hybrid warfare is increasingly being used as a tool to destabilize nations and economies, we need to prepare ourselves.”.

    Some security officials suspect that Russia could be to blame, arguing that the recent slew of incidents may be targeting European countries that have armed or financed Ukraine. In recent months, Moscow has been accused of ramping up hybrid warfare operations in Europe, from a failed drone attack on Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport in August to repeated incursions into Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. Russia continues to deny any involvement in the incidents.

    It has been revealed that the Kremlin, however, isn’t the only suspect. On Monday, French authorities accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind last month’s supermarket refrigeration attack, and the following day, the country’s foreign ministry summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris.

    Industry observers note that “We rule nothing out and will take all measures, including those we may not disclose publicly, that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot remarked on Tuesday. Such measures could include new European Union sanctions on Tehran.

    Little peace progress. Russia and Ukraine ended two days of U.S.-mediated peace talks on Wednesday with an agreement to exchange prisoners in the next few weeks. According to U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner, this will be the “biggest humanitarian release of prisoners” thus far, though exact numbers will not be finalized until Thursday.

    Sources indicate that however, the swap agreement was one of the only breakthroughs to emerge out of the talks in Abu Dhabi. Both sides remain bogged down by old sticking points, such as whether to impose a temporary cease-fire before a permanent truce and if Ukraine should relinquish Russian-occupied territory in the Donbas region.

    The lack of a European presence in Abu Dhabi may also have hindered the conference’s progress; Moscow does not want any European involvement in direct negotiations, but both Kyiv and Washington wish to add them to future talks. “We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky posted on X on Wednesday.

    Recent findings suggest that but this week’s diplomatic efforts aren’t over yet. On Thursday, Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will head to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin before traveling to Dublin for similar talks with Zelensky.

    Housing reform. Millions of Spanish residents took part in a general strike on Wednesday to protest the country’s housing affordability crisis. Backed by Spain’s two largest trade unions, the nationwide demonstrations are the first of their kind in 14 years and could help Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez steer the conversation back in his favor ahead of snap parliamentary elections later this month.

    Spain’s housing reckoning kicked off in September, when an 87-year-old Madrid resident was forcibly evicted from her home. Her struggle became the symbol of a wider conversation over skyrocketing rents, stagnant wages, and weak tenant protections across the country. Sánchez’s efforts to enact stronger tenant rights were blocked by opposition parties, though, prompting the left-wing leader to call for a snap vote.

    However, any political momentum that Sánchez earned from pursuing housing reform has come under threat in the wake of last month’s deadly train crash, which killed at least 69 people and injured more than 100 others. It was the country’s second deadly high-speed rail incident this year, raising questions about insufficient government oversight and maintenance. Sánchez’s administration is therefore likely hoping that Wednesday’s strike puts the public’s focus back on housing concerns before Spaniards head to the polls on Nov. 29.

    The nuclear status quo. Iran vowed again on Wednesday not to allow any enriched nuclear material to leave its territory, prompting global oil prices to rise after a short-term reprieve. The declaration echoes a similar directive issued by Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in May; however, Tehran reiterating the stance now could hinder efforts to restart U.S.-Iran peace talks, which largely hinge on the future of Tehran’s nuclear program.

    The White House has insisted that any final deal with Tehran must involve Iran surrendering its stockpile of highly enriched uranium and accepting curbs on its nuclear program. “Crazy Islamists in Tehran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon,” U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday in a defiant address defending the Trump administration’s controversial handling of the Iran war.

    It has been revealed that iran maintains that it does not seek a nuclear weapon and that it has the right to enrich uranium for civilian use. “We need the ​enriched material to design ships and submarines that work on nuclear energy,” Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Wednesday. However, the International Atomic Energy Agency estimated that before the United States and Israel attacked Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, Iran had 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent—a level far higher than what is needed for civilian purposes. How much highly enriched uranium the country still has today is not clear.

    Rezaei’s statement rattled energy markets, with both Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures rising 1.3 percent. In recent weeks, global oil prices dropped considerably amid hopes that the war will end soon, particularly after Trump appeared to rule out launching a fresh wave of strikes for now.

    Formal business attire may be the standard for most Japanese lawmakers, but one legislator is proving to be the exception. Last month, professional wrestler Billy Ken Kid was elected to the city of Kawanishi’s municipal assembly. Not wanting to leave his old identity behind, Billy asked city council members to approve him wearing one of his iconic wrestling masks during sessions. On Friday, the chamber greenlit Billy’s request in a “dream … come true” for the 52-year-old. However, the new lawmaker has agreed to keep his identity uninhibited when attending ceremonies outside of the assembly hall, such as memorial services.

    #6793. The petty joy of a blue election night

    The petty joy of a blue election night

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow.
    • Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.
    • Industry observers note that training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

    Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

    Industry observers note that training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”.

    Shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

    Recent findings suggest that so we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

    “If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

    “You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

    Election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

    In a recent development, neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

    So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue revealed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

    Recent findings suggest that “What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”.

    And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

    Sources indicate that peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

    In a recent development, most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Big Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood. On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his fresh network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Industry observers note that but Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

    Sources indicate that still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”.

    It has been revealed that once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

    This is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he remarked.

    So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

    Recent findings suggest that it was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. New Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

    Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

    Once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

    But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she stated, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”.

    So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory said, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”.

    That moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he said. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”.

    But by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

    • The Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m.
    • It has been revealed that the candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to defeat Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan‘s open U.S. Senate seat, a closely watched race that capped off a massive night for progressives.

    The Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m. Wednesday morning with El-Sayed leading by about seven points.

    It has been revealed that the candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, whose departure created one of the most consequential open-seat contests of the midterm elections. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, campaigned on expanding access to health care and lowering costs, while Rogers, a former congressman and House Intelligence Committee chairman, emphasized manufacturing jobs, tax cuts and his alignment with President Donald Trump.

    In a recent development, the race took an unexpected turn just two days before Election Day when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the party’s August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers during an appearance at a Detroit church.

    Industry observers note that the endorsement stunned Michigan Democrats, prompting condemnation from party leaders and resignations among Stevens’ staff. Stevens cited disagreements with El-Sayed over Israel and his campaign’s direction, while Democrats accused her of undermining their nominee in a critical Senate contest.

    El-Sayed sought to move past the controversy, urging supporters to focus on voting. His campaign reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, while Michigan Democratic officials said the endorsement had prompted an increase in volunteers. Rogers, meanwhile, highlighted Stevens’ support in the campaign’s final days.

    More than 2.3 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Monday, according to The Associated Press, raising questions about how much the late-breaking controversy could influence the outcome.

    Industry observers note that no audio? Hover over the video player, and tap the Click to Unmute button. Subtitles are also available. Closed captioning provided by Vimeo and may contain minor inconsistencies.

    Register now to watch this on-demand recording.

    Industry observers note that when Democrats take over the U.S. House and Senate in January, how will they use their new powers, and what foreign-policy issues will they prioritize? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jason Crow, a former Army Ranger who served multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and won reelection as a Democrat from Colorado’s 6th Congressional District. Crow helped lead the party’s efforts to select a diverse slate of candidates across the country, and he also helped direct their battleground and campaign strategy. He serves on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees.

    Sources indicate that the full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

    It has been revealed that when Democrats take over the U.S. House and Senate in January, how will they use their new powers, and what foreign-policy complications will they prioritize? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jason Crow, a former Army Ranger who served multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and won reelection as a Democrat from Colorado’s 6th Congressional District. Crow helped lead the party’s efforts to select a diverse slate of candidates across the country, and he also helped direct their battleground and campaign strategy. He serves on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees.

    The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

    Ravi Agrawal: I want to start with how you’re interpreting last week’s results. It was a rebuke for U.S. President Donald Trump, of course. It is less clear to me what the voters want as an alternative. So I wanted to ask you, what are the top three complications you see as takeaways that the American people want from a newly introduced Congress?

    Jason Crow: I actually think it is pretty clear what people want as an alternative. I sometimes get asked what our agenda should be come January. How about we do what we remarked we were going to do during the election? That’s the agenda—there’s no secret to this ….

    RA: Sure, but the reason why I phrased my question as I did is that the Democratic Party represents a pretty wide tent. You were part of building that strategy of selecting candidates for specific states and, on an even more micro level than that, for specific districts. So it is a wide tent, and not everyone agrees with each other.

    According to recent reports, JC: There is broad consensus on the core principles of this election. First, stop conflict with Iran, which is one of the biggest factors driving up costs in a reckless, lawless war that Americans don’t want. It’s one of the most bipartisan challenges in America right now—Republicans and Democrats alike want the endless cycle of conflict in the Middle East to stop.

    Second, stop the tariff and trade wars that are devastating farmers and ranches and businesses across this country.

    Third, roll back the cuts to the Affordable Care Act subsidies, which have devastated our healthcare system, doubled and tripled many Americans’ healthcare premiums, and in 2027 are going to result in hundreds of hospital and clinic closures.

    And fourth, go after corruption. This was the first anti-corruption election in my lifetime. Corruption became a kitchen-table issue. Americans saw that corruption has a direct impact on their lives and pocketbooks. They’ve sent a very clear mandate that they want us to go after corruption and to clean up their government.

    RA: Right. Let’s talk more about that first factor. Trump released that war with Iran without congressional approval. He conducted the Venezuela operation in January without informing Congress. There is gunboat diplomacy in the Caribbean, again, with Congress not able to do much to move the needle. Why couldn’t Congress do more, and what will actually change on that front come January?

    In a recent development, JC: Congress can do more. Congress has the power. The problem is that Congress hasn’t used that power for many decades. I think it’s really vital to note that this is not just a Donald Trump problem. For 25 years now, Congress has given blank checks in the form of faulty authorizations for the use of military force that aren’t clearly delineated and don’t have sunset provisions, which have allowed multiple presidents—Democratic and Republican alike—over multiple Congresses, also controlled by Democrats and Republicans alike, to continue a perpetual cycle of conflict.

    Industry observers note that the framers of the U.S. Constitution put an accountability loop in place: The people that decide when and how to go to war are the people’s representatives in Congress. We’re supposed to debate it, vote on it, let our constituents know where we stand, and then we’re supposed to fund it. That loop is broken. We’ve been debt funding it for over two decades, but we haven’t been debating and voting on it for over two decades, in many cases.

    Recent findings suggest that that has to end. We have the power, and that’s what we need to do in January. We have to look at the authorizations for use of military force, which we’re going to do. We’re also going to look at reforming the War Powers Act. It’s my personal belief that we should cut off funding for the Iran war and end it as quickly as we can.

    Sources indicate that RA: Critics have pointed out that it is very hard to use the power of the purse, especially when a country is already at war. Congress historically has done very little to withhold funding for wars, mostly because it will get criticized immediately. People will say you’re putting troops there in harm’s way and that you’re actively signaling to an adversary that Congress isn’t willing to do what it takes to win. How are you going to navigate that specific issue?

    Recent findings suggest that JC: They always say that. For 25 years, they’ve said, “We can’t pull out now. We just have to keep on throwing money at it.” Every year, we are told that we have to double down and keep going. Well, 25 years, $3 trillion, and 7,000 American lives later, after hundreds of thousands have been wounded and our credibility is in tatters, these wars ended poorly. So when somebody tells me we can’t possibly cut funding off, I say, “Actually, we can. Watch me.”.

    That’s different from saying that we’re going to charge the military to make sure that we wrap this up responsibly, that we’re going to do what’s called “retrograde operations,” so we protect our troops and our interests. We have the ability to do that. We have done that in the past.

    Recent findings suggest that I simply will not buy this argument that once we’re at war, we have to stick it out. It’s just not going to work. And Americans don’t want it. Americans know that that argument is a farce. What’s crazy is Donald Trump campaigned on this. He noted he was going to end this endless cycle of conflict, and then he turned his back and doubled down on it. We have to wrap it up rapidly and cut off funding.

    It has been revealed that RA: In my view, Trump basically has three options in the Iran war. One would be to escalate, even though many analysts would point out that is a terrible idea.

    Industry observers note that JC: It is a terrible idea. That’s another one of those things that has been remarked for 25 years. “We’re going to escalate to fix it and then to solve it.” How many times did we try that in Iraq and Afghanistan—15?

    RA: Right, you served in those conflicts and know this so well.

    It has been revealed that but the second option would be to do something small quickly, declare victory, and try to get out. The third would be to actively pursue diplomacy. Of that second and third option, which one would you push for?

    Sources indicate that JC: I’d push for a combination of both. We have to make sure we’re protecting ourselves and that we’re drawing down effectively. Diplomacy is really the only way out. We can’t bomb our way to a resolution. That will never work. The Iranian regime is built to withstand that.

    Our largest adversaries—Russia and China—are so happy that we are tied up in spending our stockpiles, money, and attention in Iran and not paying attention to what’s going on in the Pacific or the Russia-Ukraine conflict. They’re delighted that this is happening. So I want to pivot away from this as quickly as possible. We have the capability to do that while also protecting ourselves against a malignant Iranian regime. We have the intelligence capability. We still have the military capability to respond if we need to.

    Recent findings suggest that the only way out of this is to put together an international coalition of partners that will make sure we’re protecting the region, respecting navigation rights in the Strait of Hormuz, and preventing Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That’s what we did before and can continue to do.

    Here’s what Congress can actually do in the next two years.

    What to expect now that they’ve won big.

    Sources indicate that RA: The Republican Party managed to block an attempt to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth this week. What happens next here? Are you confident that a new House of Representatives will try to impeach Hegseth? And are you sure you think that is worth it?

    JC: It’s my opinion that we should, and I’ve been very clear to my colleagues and to leadership about that. I have a great disdain for Hegseth, but it’s not about that for me. There are a lot of people in this business that I don’t like, but I can get over that.

    According to recent reports, for me, it’s about the fact that our 1 million-plus men and women in uniform right now, who are around the world conducting combat operations and are at risk, have a failed leader at the helm of the Department of Defense. Hegseth is not just incompetent. He is corrupt and trying to change the face and the culture of the military to match his own vision, which would be a stark departure from the historic legacy of what our military should be, which is a reflection of our country and a standard-bearer of our values. As long as he is at the perch at the Pentagon, I will do everything possible to get him removed, because our service members deserve nothing less.

    Industry observers note that RA: As we said at the start, the Democrats represent a very wide tent right now. I’m curious how you’re imagining this group will go about formulating a new foreign policy. Crucially, I want to know what areas you imagine will emerge as key differences from not only the Trump era of the last two years, but also from the years under former President Joe Biden.

    JC: I think I have pretty good insight into that because, as the battleground chair for House Democrats, I visited all 12 battleground states, where I participated in countless events with farmers, doctors, nurses, and factory workers, in all sorts of communities—urban, rural, red, blue, purple.

    Industry observers note that what I can tell you is that Americans don’t want to go back. They don’t like the devastation and the chaos of this administration, but they also don’t want us to go back to where we were before. What they want us to do is move forward and to build a system that’s structured differently and that has different people at the helm that will deliver for working-class Americans.

    I highlight working-class Americans because they feel as though they have been uniquely impacted by faulty trade deals, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, deindustrialization, and technology and automation, which I agree with. They want a foreign policy that’s designed to make their lives better, that delivers for them. Every decision should be focused to that end. This shouldn’t be that hard.

    It has been revealed that RA: Can I ask you to put a little bit more meat on the bone there with some specifics? Directionally, a lot of what you’re saying sounds to me like “foreign policy for the middle class,” which was the Biden administration’s slogan.

    JC: I was getting to that. Working-class Americans want foreign policy focused on them, which is a very important organizing principle. This differentiates them from the middle class. This is actually really a key point: Working class is extremely different from middle class. When you refer to working-class people, you’re talking about a particular way of work, type of work, and way that a person lives their life.

    In America, there is a unique culture and dignity to the working class. When you say “middle class,” that means something very different in the mind of a working-class American. That was one of the defects of Biden’s policy. Almost every American thinks of themselves as middle class. But people know when they’re working class. There’s pride there.

    It has been revealed that I’m finalizing organizing principles for what I believe the future of foreign policy should look like and what we need to be focusing on. My top principle is changing the pipeline of talent. Americans don’t trust our institutions anymore. That’s very clear. And that’s hard for some people to hear.

    According to recent reports, this is why Trump won his election and why we ended up with the Department of Government Efficiency—Americans pushed back. They want significant changes to our institutions, and they don’t see themselves reflected in them. Our foreign-policy and national security apparatus is mostly run by people who went to the same two universities and grew up within 100 miles of an ocean.

    Sources indicate that that has to change. There are 200 million Americans that live in flyover country, in the heartland. There’s tremendous talent, tremendous diversity in this nation. And we have to completely alter our talent pipeline, tap into that, and help build the next generation of leadership and civil servants and diplomats who will lead us forward.

    RA: I am right in thinking here that you’re talking not just about representatives in Congress, but also about the policy incubators—the think tanks, the media, the wider ecosystem that builds the class of people who advise people like you in Congress?

    Sources indicate that JC: Exactly. That ecosystem has become very insular. It does not turn over, and it hasn’t tapped into our country. There’s very little feedback between that ecosystem and the rest of the country right now. I don’t think anyone can dispute that. Americans certainly know it’s true. There is a huge gap between what happens here in D.C. and what everyday Americans are thinking about.

    That is why trust is so broken. It’s all about people. The first step has to be getting the right people on the bus to make sure that we are restoring that trust and closing that gap.

    Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk.
    • In a recent development, we finally woke up and shook it off.
    • It has been revealed that the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

    In a recent development, we finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

    It has been revealed that the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    In a recent development, political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

    It will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and intends to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

    According to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top concern for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a newly introduced era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

    Industry observers note that it’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those issues, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

    Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

    Recent findings suggest that as great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that significant tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the Fresh Deal agenda.

    Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

    In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Sources indicate that I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most key priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this glitch there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll demonstrated that 90% of voters remarked that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

    Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Forty-five minutes before the first polls closed on Tuesday, Greg Gutfeld was still doing what Fox News does best, acknowledging reality just long enough to replace it with a culture-war hallucination.
    • Then the polls closed, and MAGA’s delusions were pulverized.
    • It has been revealed that the country woke up to results that few expected — and a long list of historic firsts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Forty-five minutes before the first polls closed on Tuesday, Greg Gutfeld was still doing what Fox News does best, acknowledging reality just long enough to replace it with a culture-war hallucination. “Gas prices are so high, I’m going to vote for the party that wanted to trans my kids,” he joked on “The Five,” adding that he didn’t see Democratic wins on the horizon. “There is no blue wave materializing,” Clay Travis, the Outkick founder and Fox contributor, posted at 3 p.m. EST, adding that Republicans were surging in Florida and the polls were about to be proven wrong yet again.

    Then the polls closed, and MAGA’s delusions were pulverized. The country that right-wing media had spent two years describing as angry, ascendant and permanently realigned voted in an avalanche that crushed years of manufactured MAGA hype. American voters told the president to take his $5,000 “Trump Dividend” checks and shove them. Elon Musk, who moved to Texas to get away from Democrats and then spent a reported $150 million to deliver the Lone Star State for Republicans, saw his early Tuesday post urging people to vote red disappear from his profile by Wednesday.

    It has been revealed that the country woke up to results that few expected — and a long list of historic firsts. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman governor in American history. Michigan sent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Washington as the first Muslim senator. Newly introduced Hampshire elected Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man in the Senate. New Mexico made Deb Haaland the first Native American woman governor, and Peggy Flanagan became Minnesota’s first Native American woman senator. Texas elected Gina Hinojosa over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott — the state’s first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Ohio got its first woman governor in Dr. Amy Acton. South Carolina tapped Dr. Annie Andrews as its first elected woman senator. Democrats won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in 94 years. While votes are still being counted in key races, solid majorities in both the Senate and House are assured, and Democrats are set to make Hakeem Jeffries the country’s first Black speaker.

    Even the Fresh York Post, Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid and a loyal Trump house organ, refused to mince words on its front page: “Trump suffers historic rebuke as Dems romp in midterms,” with “BLUE TSUNAMI” blaring beneath it. On “Fox and Friends” Wednesday morning, Ainsley Earhart warned viewers that “your wallet and your way of life” are now in the crosshairs.

    The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment.

    It is no surprise that Trump 2.0, stripped of its previous establishment Republican guardrails like Mike Pence and Mitch McConnell, has culminated in such total structural collapse. The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment. Right-wing media spent years confusing its ability to dominate a conversation with its ability to represent a country. When Tuesday’s returns exposed the difference, its leading voices reached for almost everything except accountability. They blamed immigration. They blamed insufficient restrictions on voting. They blamed each other. Alex Jones even decided Trump might secretly be a Democrat.

    Industry observers note that for the network’s election night coverage, Fox News seated former Latest York Mayor Bill de Blasio between two of Trump’s former press secretaries, Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt, and he told them to their faces that they were “missing the plot.” He stated, “The American people are looking at a war they do not believe in, and they did not authorize. They’re looking at prices that are making it impossible for middle-class people, let alone working-class people, to live.”.

    Trump, watching at the White House, raged on Truth Social — “Why does FoxNews have deBlasio” — and seethed at the panel’s lone liberal: “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me.” After Gutfeld read the president’s text on air — which is as good a diagram as exists of what Fox News is now: a suggestion box the president monitors live — Tarlov answered on X, not on Truth Social: “Reality is a tricky thing,” and the president “should get better at dealing with it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on Newsmax, things were somehow worse. Political strategist Dick Morris argued that Trump’s problem was effectively excessive success: He had solved the major problems that would otherwise motivate Republican voters. The influencer ecosystem, meanwhile, went straight for the circular firing squad, and every faction picked a different target.

    Jones, livestreaming as the returns buried his movement, remarked Trump himself is the plant: “I think he’s a Democrat. I’m 100% at war with Trump. He’s not that r*tarded. He did this on purpose. I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them.” Benny Johnson and Libs of TikTok reached for the great replacement theory, and Fox’s Lawrence Jones supplied the broadcast version, surveying Texas and concluding, “Texas, there is a lesson here. Don’t be so welcoming.”.

    So much for celebrating people voting with their feet and the U-Hauls leaving California.

    Laura Loomer went straight doomer: “America is over and so is the American Dream.” Others blamed Sen. John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE Act and shrink the electorate further, as though the answer to such a broad repudiation were fewer voters. The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro posted the “everything is fine” fire GIF — “Just checking in to see how things are goi—” — and the Federalist’s Sean Davis answered with the hot-dog-suit meme, the one where the man in the costume insists everyone else is the problem.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    According to recent reports, the recriminations got personal fast. Rep.     #6779. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation
