    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
    • The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
    • The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

    The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

    The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

    It has been revealed that “The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition states.

    Industry observers note that trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

    In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

    In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

    Sources indicate that immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

    The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

    The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a upcoming removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

    Industry observers note that last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

    A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

    The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

    The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

    The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Sources indicate that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

    Sources indicate that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

    Sources indicate that when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

    In a recent development, over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

    The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

    In a recent development, the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

    In a recent development, thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

    Sources indicate that thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

    Have you seen a cuter pair of workout shorts? I love the retro design with colorblocking and contrasting trims along with the mesh panels at the sides and hem. It’s one of the few workout shorts I wear just as frequently outside of the gym as I do to break a sweat. Pair it with a simple white tank (or top in any other color featured in the short) and flip-flops, and you have the perfect vintage activewear fit. On colder outings, throw your favorite sporty hoodie on top for a good complement.

    In a recent development, I’m also a big fan of the length: The approximately 5-inch inseam and roomy leg openings with notched hems at the sides give a leg-slimming effect and are also just super comfortable. It also makes sure I don’t accidentally show too much skin while running in my neighborhood or picking up weights at the gym. An added layer of protection there is the built-in brief, which, unlike many I’ve encountered, doesn’t feel like it's giving me a constant wedgie (I’ve literally cut them out of my shorts before, but I barely notice it in this short).

    In a recent development, another bonus? The mesh paneling I mentioned earlier is as stylish as it is breathable. Even when I throw it on for a run on a treadmill in a stuffy gym, things stay feeling light and airy.

    It has been revealed that I only wish this short came in more colors—I would genuinely purchase them all. Right now, you can snag it in two color combos, but I’d love to see a few more and maybe even a neutral option.

    According to recent reports, if you're looking for a buttery-soft workout fit, this biker short from Beyond Yoga is your best friend. The brand itself is a favorite among our fashion team, and that's because the fabrics, which are made from super soft polyester and elastane, are never tight and constricting, always smooth and soft (yet still contouring and flattering!).

    Yes, the short is awesome for all sorts of workouts, but we also love it for running errands and, dare we say it, lounging, as it looks so cute with every outfit and feels so comfortable for all-day wear. Plus, it's moisture-wicking during sweaty workouts. Speaking of sunny days, the short also has built-in UV protection, because we're all about staying protected from the sun here.

    The Spacedye Biker Short is also one of the longest options on this list, so it's a solid choice if you're looking for something with a bit more leg coverage.

    Sources indicate that I often wear this short to yoga, but it's compressive enough that it doesn't budge when I wear it for a run or to higher-intensity classes. According to stylist Kristen Saladino, the high-waisted fit makes you feel super tucked-in and secure without feeling constricted. And, if you need a larger size, this short goes all the way up to a 4XL.

    I do wish there were more colors to choose from. As of now, the brand only offers two core colors in this short.

    Recent findings suggest that sure, we love the lululemon short for running, but the Norvan Short from Arc'teryx is built for the trails—and that’s exactly what we use it for. Lauture gives this fitted short a major thumbs-up for feeling super light and breathable, especially on long runs. It’s made from 100% polyester, so it’s airy and helps keep you cool by letting moisture escape and regulating your body temp. And if things do get sweaty, the built-in moisture-wicking brief (with antimicrobial treatment) helps manage odor—so you don’t have to stress.

    In a recent development, got loose keys or headphones? There's a discreet zippered back pocket that fits the essentials, like gels, electrolyte packs—you name it. It also has a reflective logo to help with visibility if you're running after dark. Another plus: the split side hem gives you a full range of motion, which is great for picking up the pace.

    Sources indicate that our only real gripe is that we wish the waistband were a bit thicker for more tummy support. It’s also low-rise, which might not be everyone’s thing—but Lauture said she was surprised by how comfortable it felt and that it stayed put during her runs.

    Sources indicate that in my experience, it's difficult to find flowy workout shorts that don't show too much skin, but this option from Alo shifts that paradigm. It's light and airy with its woven material, but it doesn't have any open seams, so you don't have to worry about the wind catching it in the wrong way (IYKYK). Plus, it has a built-in brief, which is awesome for added protection.

    Recent findings suggest that I also love the thick elastic waistband, which not only adds a fun design element, but hits at the perfect height on our stomach to offer a nice contouring effect. There's also an invisible side pocket to store all your small essentials while on the go.My favorite part about this short is that it's never clingy, so it doesn't ride up the thigh or need constant readjusting while you're working out. I’ve owned it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout as well as an hour-long cross-training workout, and I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it. It's roomy, but also holds you in. Plus, the fabric dries super fast, so you're in good hands if you get super sweaty.It does run one size significant, which you should note when adding to cart. However, if you like shorts that are roomier, I can confirm that this one still gets high marks even when it's a size too big. In my experience, it still felt full-coverage, airy, and lightweight.

    Industry observers note that patagonia’s Baggies Short is a warm-weather favorite among our editors—especially the ones who love spending time outdoors, like myself. The short fared exceptionally well during hot hikes over the summer but does just as well in the offseason indoors or while active outside.

    It’s easy to throw on, thanks to its comfy fit that completely avoids any unwanted cling (no camel toe here, thank you very much). Plus, it’s made from quick-drying, breathable nylon, so I never have to worry about feeling weighed down. I’m personally stoked to wear this short again while hiking in Cotopaxi National Park in Ecuador.

    It has been revealed that while it definitely has a sporty vibe, it’s versatile enough to wear around the city, too. In black, it feels laid-back and low-key—perfect for running errands without looking like you just left the gym. Toss on an oversized sweatshirt or a longline sports bra, and you’ve got an effortless, off-duty look. And if you get caught in the rain or decide to take a dip? No stress—it’s water-repellent, so it won’t stay soaked.

    In a recent development, the 5-inch inseam is another win: not too long, not too short—just the right amount of leg without worrying about coverage. Prefer something shorter? The Baggie also comes in a 2.5-inch version, which is great if you want a more cropped fit.

    In a recent development, fabric is everything when it comes to workout shorts—look for lightweight, sweat-wicking materials that move with you, not against you. According to Saladino, it's best to steer clear of cotton when looking for athletic shorts, as it doesn't wick away moisture as well as materials like polyester and nylon. After all, you want to make sure you're staying totally dry in your workout shorts (because who wants sweat stains down there?).

    Sources indicate that most shorts on this list are high-rise, which we found to have the most coverage and look the most flattering during our workouts, as they offer flattering tummy control. Many high-rise shorts also have a drawstring, which helps you customize the fit so it doesn't slip down or ride up while you're getting a sweat on. Some of the options we tried were low-rise, but we ended up ditching most of them because we didn't love the fit. However, the Arc'teryx pair on this list is low-rise, and we actually love that it sits nicely on our hips and looks flattering.

    When it comes to the best length for workout shorts, you want to think about the inseam length, AKA the distance between the crotch area and the bottom of the short. There are some longer options for those who prefer more leg coverage (ideal for burpees and squats!), and super short options on this list if you like a lightweight mini short for running or walking. After testing, we prefer something right in the middle that makes us feel nimble but also provides coverage, like our favorite of the bunch, The Gym People High Waist Shorts.

On the other hand, the Arc'teryx pair is low-rise, super light, and has a snug fit, making it ideal for running since it feels weightless and doesn't slow us down.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

    Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

    The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

    Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

    Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

    It has been revealed that A newcomer to electoral politics, she rapidly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

    In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

    Industry observers note that running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch revealed he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

    According to recent reports, this year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

    Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

    Latest Update: Huang Out at Nvidia

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.
    • Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.
    • Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

    Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

    Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

    Sources indicate that huang has been seen as the face of the global artificial intelligence race. His company is the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips, making Nvidia a critical part of U.S. national security and a sought-after partner of China. Huang himself is among the world’s wealthiest people, with an estimated net worth of around $162 billion prior to his recent scandal.

    Over the past two years, Huang has also become a close friend of U.S. President Donald Trump, whose administration has made advancing AI a cornerstone of its agenda. Notably, Huang successfully petitioned the White House last December to relax some restrictions on Nvidia sales to China in exchange for the U.S. government receiving a 25 percent cut of the profits.

    Sources indicate that but in just two weeks, Huang’s public image has collapsed. Late last month, the Upcoming York Times reported that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying for Beijing was in a “close relationship” with Huang. The alleged spy, Alice Huang, was an executive at a Singapore-based data center manufacturer, Megaspeed, which the U.S. Commerce Department began suspecting in 2024 of helping China to smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted AI chips.

    Recent findings suggest that nvidia shares plummeted in the wake of the news, even as Beijing denied involvement. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday.

    Recent findings suggest that however, the scandal didn’t end there. On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had had a separate affair with Kimberly Powell, the manufacturer’s vice president of healthcare. That relationship may have violated the company’s code of conduct. Huang has not publicly acknowledged the second affair.

    In a recent development, the dual allegations appear to have been enough to force Huang to step down. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress ahead of the U.S. holiday of Thanksgiving over the espionage scandal. And Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress has agreed to serve as interim CEO until a replacement is named.

    Industry observers note that nvidia’s change in leadership, though, has yet to assuage global markets. Organization shares plunged as much as 14 percent when trading opened on Thursday, extending a crisis that has already wiped out more than $1 trillion from Nvidia’s market value. Some initial gains were made later in the day but not enough to reverse the damage.

    Nvidia’s board has said there is “no reason to believe” that Huang’s actions compromised U.S. national security or firm secrets, but it has introduced an independent investigation. And on Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong issued a statement saying that the company takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously” and will work “constructively and transparently with the U.S. government.”.

    Trump, meanwhile, praised Huang on Thursday, writing on Truth Social that he had done a “fantastic job” with Nvidia.

    A seat at the table. Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday to allow European representatives to join the next round of direct Ukraine peace talks. Giving Europe a seat at the table marks a significant win for Kyiv and Washington, which have both pushed for greater European involvement in negotiations. However, the concession could also spell trouble for future talks, as Moscow remains largely at odds with its European counterparts.

    According to recent reports, “We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the U.S. administration as a whole to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” Putin told U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on Thursday. At the same time, the Russian leader warned that any push for the deployment of European troops to Ukraine after a peace deal is inked would trigger renewed fighting.

    Witkoff and Kushner will now head to Dublin for similar talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The potential of European involvement in the peace process will almost certainly be on the agenda, but Zelensky is also likely to bring up newly introduced reports of Starlink disruptions in Ukraine.

    Industry observers note that zelensky on Thursday accused the U.S.-based company of placing speed restrictions on its Starshield military-grade services, affecting how its drone interceptors operate. The last time that such limits were detected, Zelensky resumed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in direct opposition to Trump’s wishes. Kyiv and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had both accused the Trump administration of orchestrating that incident, which the White House denied.

    According to recent reports, academic scandal. Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation to parliament on Thursday in the wake of a scandal over his academic credentials. It is unclear when his departure will take effect; however, experts expect the incident to deliver another blow to the tenuous alliance between former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo and current President Prabowo Subianto.

    Calls for Gibran’s impeachment first intensified last month, when the country’s Constitutional Court found that the vice president did not possess the necessary credentials to hold power. In Indonesia, lawmakers must have a high school diploma to run for office. Gibran claimed to have finished grade 12 at a school in Australia, but the court ruled that the degree was not equivalent to an Indonesian senior high school certificate. Two weeks later, the country’s Supreme Court backed that ruling by revoking Gibran’s equivalency document.

    Sources indicate that gibran was elected in 2024 largely as a symbol of the precarious truce between his father, Jokowi, and Prabowo. His removal could therefore further fracture that fragile alliance. Just last week, Indonesian authorities detained three senior police officials suspected of wiretapping the president and dozens of other prominent figures. Among those arrested was Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was a known loyalist of Jokowi.

    Gaza hospital attack. An Israeli airstrike targeted the main hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis overnight on Thursday, killing at least six people, including a teenager, and injuring at least 20 others. Locals reported two missiles damaging a building containing surgical wards at Nasser Hospital. The attack marked the latest violation of the region’s precarious Gaza cease-fire, which took effect in October 2025.

    In a recent development, according to Israel’s military, the hospital strike was part of an operation targeting Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom Israeli forces described as the “commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade.” Israel claimed that Abu Ismail had turned Nasser Hospital into his headquarters and was using the facility as a base of operations. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using civilian infrastructure as human shields. The militant group has denied doing so.

    Recent findings suggest that since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023, Israeli troops have attacked Nasser Hospital at least seven times, according to hospital officials. The use of medical centers for military purposes and the targeting of such sites are both considered violations of international law. “Gaza’s health facilities are lifelines for its ​people,” World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X on Thursday. “They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked.”.

    According to recent reports, the Finnish Embassy in Canberra temporarily closed its doors on Tuesday for a one-day internal planning and staff sauna event. However, what was meant to be a routine disruption instead appeared to upend the internet, with a deluge of memes jokingly bemoaning the closure. Local swimming pools offered their services for those suffering, a Dutch esports league complained about the lockout, and even American Airlines unveiled a snap sale on flights to Europe for emotional support.

    The embassy, meanwhile, took the public’s outcry in stride. “After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened,” the facility posted on social media on Wednesday, marking the event with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.

    Sources indicate that alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family declared.

    In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

    As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

    In a recent development, “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

    When McDermott revealed his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

    Sources indicate that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

    He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

    He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

    Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a upcoming life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

    “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

    Sources indicate that as he stated, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

    It has been revealed that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

    “The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

    McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

    “Jim McDermott was as massive as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

    Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

    Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

    Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

    Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

    According to recent reports, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth narrowly escaped an impeachment effort this week, but questions remain over his job security.

    The push to impeach Hegseth, led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, was blocked by Republicans in the House on Tuesday. The House voted 211 to 204 on a motion to refer the articles of impeachment to the House Judiciary Committee, which effectively tanked the chances of Hegseth getting impeached—for now. Eleven Democrats missed the vote, which helped House Republicans pass the motion by seven votes.

    In a recent development, but Hegseth’s troubles are far from over as Republicans continue to contend with the fallout from their disastrous performance in the midterms, which was driven in part by voter discontent over the economic consequences of the Iran war. In Washington, Hegseth is seen as the face of that war, as well as other controversial military actions that President Donald Trump has taken in Latin America, putting the defense secretary’s future in question as the political landscape shifts.

    What’s next for Hegseth. Democrats could launch another effort to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. “This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next House speaker, said after the impeachment vote this week.

    Recent findings suggest that democrats will have the votes in the House to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. But they’re less likely to garner the support of enough Republicans in the Senate to convict and remove the defense secretary.

    Whether Democrats pursue impeachment or not, Hegseth will be under a microscope. Democrats have been clear that they will leverage their oversight powers to investigate him on everything from the Iran war and the military operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to the lethal strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats near Latin America. Even some Republicans in recent days have suggested that he should just resign and stated that they want more answers on the Iran war.

    Trump has backed Hegseth so far and signaled that he doesn’t plan to fire him. As long as the president stands by him, Hegseth might be able to save his job. People have been “predicting that Secretary Hegseth would be on his way out” since the Signalgate controversy, mentioned Peter Feaver, a professor of political science and public policy at Duke University.

    In a recent development, “He’s shown that he’s quite adept at holding on to his position because he’s maintained the confidence of the one person that matters in the administration, and that’s President Trump,” Feaver said. “I don’t see evidence that he has lost President Trump’s confidence. If anything, Trump is more fulsome in his expressions of support for Secretary Hegseth.”.

    Hegseth vs. Congress. Hegseth, a former Fox News host, went on the offensive in the past week, launching a campaign-style media blitz against his opponents in Congress, posting about it on social media, and delivering a fiery speech at a rare press conference from the Pentagon. It was indicative of the unusually partisan approach that Hegseth has taken to his role. Some watchdogs have also suggested that Hegseth’s messaging campaign violated federal law.

    Defense secretaries are meant to be political animals who are “very nonpartisan” but “really wily at working Congress,” Feaver said. “Hegseth has not fit that mold,” Feaver added, describing him as the “most partisan” defense secretary in modern times. While this has helped Hegseth maintain Trump’s trust, the defense secretary “also answers to Congress,” Feaver said, especially when it comes to the defense budget that the Defense Department relies on.

    Recent findings suggest that the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual defense policy bill that dictates yearly U.S. military spending levels, is stalled in Congress. The White House has been pressing Congress to pass a record budget request of $1.5 trillion, but Hegseth’s recent attack campaign may have made this even harder than it already was in a lame-duck session.

    It also doesn’t set the Pentagon up “for success in the last two years in terms of working with the upcoming Congress,” Feaver mentioned. Trump on Thursday called on Senate Republicans to “IMMEDIATELY” pass $350 billion in defense spending via reconciliation before Democrats take over.

    Hegseth is used to a less active Congress, but that’s about to change with Democrats at the helm. “There’s a saying in the military—you don’t fight against the terrain,” Feaver said.

    Sources indicate that russian Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev died aged 66 in Moscow, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Wednesday. Darchiev had been posted in Washington since March 2025 but returned to Moscow to seek treatment for a chronic illness, CNN reported.

    Erik Slavin, the former editor in chief of the Pentagon-funded newspaper Stars and Stripes, declared on Wednesday that he would be joining the Atlantic as a staff writer covering the U.S. military. Slavin was fired from his post at Stars and Stripes in August for alleged insubordination after he defended the publication’s editorial independence.

    What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

    Sources indicate that russia-Ukraine stalemate continues. Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, failed to yield a major breakthrough this week, save for an agreement for Russia and Ukraine to exchange prisoners of war. The broader sticking points that have dogged the conflict remain, including the prospect of a temporary cease-fire and both sides’ territorial claims on the front lines.

    The Kremlin appears unwilling to cede any ground, with lead Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky telling reporters after the talks that “every square foot of land will be returned to Russia one way or another.” U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday before heading to Dublin for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that same day. Witkoff told reporters in Moscow that European officials will join the next round of talks—a potentially significant step given that Putin has long resisted any European role in talks to end the war.

    Recent findings suggest that vance reassigned. Trump unveiled in a Truth Social post on Thursday that he has ordered Vice President J.D. Vance “to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.” instead of working on negotiations with Iran. Vance has been leading those negotiations and was reportedly set to meet with a senior Iranian security official to try to end the war.

    Sources indicate that “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!,” Trump wrote.

    As John reported, Vance last week blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm losses in a rare public statement.

    Recent findings suggest that huang’s out. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday—the latest twist in a weekslong scandal that has unleashed turmoil at the $4 trillion manufacturer whose semiconductor chips have become indispensable to the development of artificial intelligence. Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy and is accused of having another one with a subordinate at Nvidia.

    Recent findings suggest that huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has overseen the company’s rise into a technology behemoth and has himself become the face of the global AI race. His departure has implications far beyond the company or any one country. Rishi explains why in his piece on the saga.

    Pro-Palestinian protesters attend a rally at Trinity College in Dublin, Ireland, on Nov. 10 during a visit by former U.S. President Joe Biden.Li Mangmang/Xinhua via Getty Images.

    Tuesday, Nov. 17: Trump arrives in Manila for the ASEAN-U.S. special summit and Quad leaders summit.

    Industry observers note that wednesday, Nov. 18: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economic leaders meeting begins in Shenzhen, China.

    In a recent development, thursday, Nov. 19: The International Court of Justice is scheduled to pronounce its final judgment on accusations of genocide against Myanmar over its campaign against Rohingya Muslims.

    According to recent reports, friday, Nov. 20: The European Union hosts the EU-U.K. summit.

    Recent findings suggest that “My analogy would be … the Titanic hit the iceberg on Nov. 3, and I came up with a life raft, and they noted, ‘No thanks, we’re going to stick on the Titanic.’”.

    Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
    • The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

    The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

    He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

    During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the complications were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

    Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from upcoming software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin stated “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

    Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

    “This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

    The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

    Mullin stated the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

    “We need someone to come in and build the whole system,” Mullin noted. “Nickel and diming it together does not work.”.

    According to recent reports, thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for “cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.”.

    Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.”.

    Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

    The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight prepares. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

    The committee’s majority noted Friday’s outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a fresh one was built.

    Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., mentioned in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

    “Technology challenges related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell noted.

    Cantwell is poised to take the committee’s gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

    In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and noted their committee would “thoroughly review the challenges that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

    Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

    Sources indicate that at glitch in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have stated they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Like many U.S. presidents before him, Donald Trump is responding to a final midterm election drubbing by heading for foreign shores—to a region that has been far from top of mind over the past two years.

    Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. At the latter, he will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third time this year. In Manila, Trump is expected to meet with the other leaders in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue—between the United States, Australia, Japan, and India—for the first time in his second term.

    Like many U.S. presidents before him, Donald Trump is responding to a final midterm election drubbing by heading for foreign shores—to a region that has been far from top of mind over the past two years.

    Sources indicate that trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. At the latter, he will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third time this year. In Manila, Trump is expected to meet with the other leaders in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue—between the United States, Australia, Japan, and India—for the first time in his second term.

    Trump will make those trips under the shadow of his political diminishment at home, with last week’s elections leading to the Democratic Party’s control of Congress starting in January and giving them the ability to block Trump’s legislative agenda.

    Sources indicate that “It is often the case when a president ventures to a major trip in Asia, a long domestic shadow casts its darkness over the trip,” said Kurt Campbell, chairman and co-founder of The Asia Group, a geopolitical advisory firm in Washington, D.C. “This is another case of just massive overhang from domestic politics that are going to shape everything that he does,” added Campbell, who previously served as deputy secretary of state and Indo-Pacific coordinator on the National Security Council under former U.S. President Joe Biden.

    But Trump is equally likely to try and push past that dynamic, mentioned Mike Kuiken, vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a bipartisan panel that advises U.S. lawmakers on China. “The reality is that Trump is weaker at home politically, so I think he’s going to feel very motivated to project power and confidence,” said Kuiken, who is also a distinguished visiting fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution.

    In a recent development, trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Kuiken said. “There’s going to be red carpets, and flowers, and parades, and military equipment all over the place, so this is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy.”.

    Substance, there may be less of.

    In a recent development, experts predict that in his meeting with Xi, Trump will seek to maintain the status quo between the world’s two largest economies—whether with their trade truce (which the two countries just extended until mid-January), their nascent dialogue on artificial intelligence, or their tit-for-tat export controls on U.S. semiconductor chips and China’s critical minerals.

    Sources indicate that “I think at least the Chinese expect that he will be more desirous of preserving calm on the diplomatic front now that he is politically weakened and presumably will not want to see the stock market dips or other things that would erode his position even further,” mentioned Hal Brands, a professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who also serves on the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. The commission, incidentally, is set to publish its annual report to Congress on Wednesday—the same day that Trump is scheduled to touch down in Shenzhen.

    The midterm result “probably makes Trump more interested in getting massive, good international headlines to help him restore a sense of momentum around his presidency,” said Brands, who is also a frequent Foreign Policy contributor.

    Industry observers note that trump’s semiconductor position may also be muddied by the turmoil around Nvidia, the chipmaking giant at the center of the U.S. export control debate. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned on Thursday after news emerged of his extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy as well as with one of his subordinates at the company.

    According to recent reports, huang cultivated close personal ties with Trump and attended both of his previous meetings with Xi in Beijing and Washington along with other tech CEOs. Last December, Huang successfully petitioned the Trump administration to relax some restrictions on sales of the tech giant’s second-tier chips to China—giving the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of some sales in the process.

    The Nvidia drama is already causing tension in the U.S.-China relationship. “The U.S. should stop fabricating the ‘Chinese spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing on Thursday.

    Sources indicate that but the Nvidia elephant in the room is likely to be mutually ignored—or promptly swept under the rug—when Trump and Xi meet. “There’s no gain for Trump in making an glitch of this and even less gain for Xi in making an issue of it, and so I would be kind of surprised if it came up in their bilateral meeting,” Kuiken stated. However, Xi is likely to stress that any further tightening of chip export controls through proposed legislation would invite retaliation from Beijing. “I wouldn’t be shocked if Xi were to try to find ways of reminding President Trump: ‘Oh, it’s wonderful what we’ve achieved together over the last year, would be such a shame if anything were to happen to disrupt this productive relationship,’” Kuiken added.

    Sources indicate that there’s also the prospect of a trilateral meeting of Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump noted that he thinks he will meet the two leaders in Shenzhen to discuss “a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he said on Sunday. But Beijing appears to be wary of the implications of such a meeting, given its long-standing reluctance to commit to arms control.

    “If the Xi-Putin-Trump meeting happens, it will only happen because the Chinese have received sufficient guarantees that it’ll be utterly devoid of substance,” Brands noted. “The things that Trump wants to discuss are a settlement in Ukraine and nuclear arms control. The Chinese have no intention of being put on the hook as a responsible party in bringing the war in Ukraine to an end, and they have no interest in a trilateral nuclear arms control negotiation,” he added. “They would want to make this as scripted and formulaic as possible.”.

    For Beijing, simply having and hosting the meeting holds a degree of appeal. “When we were in China, we heard over and over again about how the Chinese really liked President Trump’s ‘G-2’ framework,” Kuiken remarked. “What happens when it becomes sort of a G-3 framework where China effectively has two seats at the table? Because you know Putin’s seat is essentially China’s seat.”.

    It has been revealed that putin, as the leader who first floated the meeting, appears more amenable to discussing both nuclear weapons and Ukraine but will likely look to focus more on the latter, said Edgard Kagan, a senior advisor and chair of China studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C. “This was originally a Putin idea,” Kagan told reporters in a briefing earlier this week. “I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like.”.

    Sources indicate that then there’s the Quad, which will be convening a leaders’ meeting on the sidelines of ASEAN before Trump heads to Shenzhen. It will mark the first and likely final time that Trump meets the other leaders of the security grouping—Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi—together in his current term.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been the flag-bearer for the Quad thus far, having attended and convened multiple meetings with his counterparts over the past two years. Trump’s participation is unlikely to amount to more than a box-checking exercise, experts remarked.

    “I don’t think the president can hide the fact that he’s not terribly enthusiastic about the gathering,” Campbell mentioned, adding that the Trump administration’s notable lack of preparation for meetings with traditional U.S. allies and partners will not be lost on their leaders. “If you compare how he prepares and thinks about a meeting with Putin or Xi, or even potentially with [North Korean dictator] Kim Jong Un, there just is a noticeable difference, and that’s not lost on Asian interlocutors,” Campbell added.

    There are limits to what the other countries that form ASEAN will seek to extract from Trump—to the extent that they get to engage with him at all. “They have probably learned by now that the most effective place to engage this administration is never in a multilateral format but is actually a bilateral format, so I think that the more interesting meetings are the sidebars,” noted Kuiken. “These meetings are probably more likely to be the places where these countries choose to engage, as opposed to trying to box in the U.S in some sort of larger regional discussion or engagement.”.

    Sources indicate that the White House has not yet released a full schedule for Trump’s visit, though a bilateral meeting in Manila with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appears to be in the cards and others could materialize closer to the date.

    In a recent development, trade is likely to be high on Asian leaders’ lists of priorities. “Some of the tariffs that he has imposed on these countries are pretty staggering, and so I think those countries now may feel emboldened to compel or urge Trump to revisit these things,” Kuiken noted. “It’ll be interesting to see if they decide to play that card in this first meeting, or if they decide to hold back for a later engagement that’s sort of quieter and a little more underneath the radar.”.

    Sources indicate that according to Campbell, the major question on every leader’s mind will be the resolution of a conflict that none of them are directly involved in. “We all know that the Iran war had an impact on this [U.S. midterm] election, but it is starting to have very substantial impacts across Asia,” he noted, mentioning supplies of key industrial inputs such as helium, sulfur, and diesel that have been disrupted by the war. “When the war started eight months ago, it was at a moment in which most countries had maximum reserves in many of these areas. Those reserves are now gone,” he added. “So [Trump] is going to be in countries and meeting with leaders—the Philippines, Indonesia, other Southeast Asian countries that are being battered by higher costs associated with energy and the like.”.

    Ultimately, however, Campbell said those leaders will already be starting to look past Trump.

    “I think what they see [from the midterms] is a pretty clear rejection of a style of politics in the United States and a rejection of the United States as an authoritarian leader-led country,” he said. “And so, the biggest manifestation is going to be Asian interlocutors seeking out other power sources in Washington.”.

    #6742. The Missing Critical Minerals Investment

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2372 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The Missing Critical Minerals Investment

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tom Moerenhout is a Professor at Columbia University’s School of Public and International Affairs, Director of Critical Materials at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, and Executive Director at the Geneva Platform for Resilient Value Chains.
    • Kevin Brunelli is a Nonresident Fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy and previously served in the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Supply Chains at the U.S.
    • To Catch Up to China, America and Its Allies Must Dig.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tom Moerenhout is a Professor at Columbia University’s School of Public and International Affairs, Director of Critical Materials at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, and Executive Director at the Geneva Platform for Resilient Value Chains.

    Kevin Brunelli is a Nonresident Fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy and previously served in the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Supply Chains at the U.S. Department of State.

    To Catch Up to China, America and Its Allies Must Dig.

    Tom Moerenhout and Kevin Brunelli.

    The United States and its allies are finally taking supply chains for critical minerals seriously. China has spent the last three decades building a dominant share of global mineral production, and the export controls Beijing has introduced periodically since 2023 have made clear just how dangerous it is for other countries to rely on China for access to materials that are essential components of semiconductors, defense technologies, and automobiles.

    Industry observers note that washington and European capitals are now trying to minimize their exposure. Alongside private firms, these governments have begun investing in both upstream industries including mines, refineries, and recycling infrastructure and downstream industries such as magnets and batteries. The bulk of their efforts so far have focused on mines already in operation or close to it and on refining. It is true that the United States and Europe do not have sufficient facilities to process raw ore into specialized chemicals or refined materials and that building more refining facilities will help reduce their reliance on China and alleviate immediate supply chain concerns.

    According to recent reports, but this is a temporary fix. Refining facilities are valuable only if they have a steady, long-term supply of raw materials. That, in turn, requires new mines, especially as advanced industries demand ever more minerals. Because building a mine takes roughly 20 years, ensuring a long-term supply of minerals requires investing in new mines now. China, which is committed to maintaining its supply chain dominance, has been willing to allocate substantial capital to such ventures. Japan has, too, ever since China blocked exports of critical minerals to the country amid a dispute over the Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands) in 2010, which pushed Tokyo to start the long process of disentangling its own supply chains. But Japan still has a long way to go; after 15 years of investing, the country has reduced its dependence on China for rare earths from about 90 percent to between 65 and 70 percent—not nearly enough to supply its own needs, much less those of its allies.

    Industry observers note that in short, investing in refining is necessary but insufficient. To avoid future supply chain vulnerabilities, the United States and its allies, especially those in the G-7, must also start building a pipeline of fresh mines. These investments are long bets, and they are risky. But when successful, they reap high rewards.

    Sources indicate that the United States and its allies significantly outperform China in mineral exploration. Australian and Canadian firms alone account for roughly one-third of global exploration spending. But the vast majority of geological prospects never become operating mines. This is not for lack of financing in prospecting but because of the many financial disincentives and risks that appear once a mining project moves forward.

    The initial stages of mining development rely chiefly on a unique ecosystem of mining companies called “juniors,” so called because they have a small market cap, focus exclusively on one or a few projects, and are nowhere large enough to list on major stock exchanges. Most of them list in Australia or Canada and concentrate on the initial high-risk exploration stages. Geological uncertainty makes betting on junior ventures extraordinarily risky, but if a mineral deposit proves to have significant reserves, the junior can sell the project or bring in a newly introduced partner, and that payout is large.

    It has been revealed that yet in the next stages, investors tend to lose patience or run out of capital. Although initial prospecting is relatively cheap, subsequent feasibility studies that estimate a deposit’s size, engineering needs, costs, and expected returns can easily run into the tens of millions of dollars, in addition to the costs of drilling, engineering, permitting, and development planning. Commercial lenders stay away because these projects have no immediate revenue, no assets to offer as collateral, and no guarantees they will even be viable. The risk, in short, is too high to take for uncertain returns. Large mining companies also avoid these projects because they face pressure from shareholders to provide maximum returns. Even as demand for minerals has risen, the share of revenue that major mining companies have reinvested in fresh development has stayed flat.

    Without outside financing, juniors cannot complete the studies needed to attract additional financing for construction, even if they have found a promising deposit. As single-asset companies, they have no other cash flow or assets to offer as collateral for additional loans. This moment is often referred to as the “valley of death.” Many companies looking for a way out of this predicament have turned to one reliable source of investment: China. Chinese companies are much more willing to take on this type of risk and provide the necessary capital to advance mining projects, and they are often the only viable option for juniors. Thus, China’s dominance in global supply chains relies on Western companies’ exploration. It endures not because China offers more competitive terms but because at a key financing stage, it is the only game in town.

    China has been expanding its supply pipeline for critical minerals for decades. In 2025, it spent a record $32 billion on metals and mining projects through its Belt and Road Initiative, breaking the previous year’s record of $21 billion. Chinese firms are also willing to invest in equity, buying ownership stakes in companies that come with no guaranteed returns. Additional spending takes the form of resources-for-infrastructure deals, by which China funds infrastructure such as ports, energy facilities, and railways in mineral-rich countries in exchange for a share in the profits of mining projects—which Chinese companies and state banks may also help finance. By investing in a broad portfolio of mineral projects across several countries, Chinese firms can let the profits of those that succeed cover the losses of those that fail.

    In a recent development, apart from capital, the most notable part of China’s mining strategy is know-how. Because failure is so common, the ability to identify deposits with the highest potential to deliver is crucial. Beijing relies on specialized state-owned enterprises, geological firms, private companies, and government officials to vet projects and work with host governments to secure permits, infrastructure, and delivery. The only G-7 country that maintains a comparable on-the-ground presence for mining projects is Japan, in countries such as Australia, Canada, Peru, and Uzbekistan. These projects are intended to secure critical minerals that can support Japan’s industries, but they are presently insufficient to meet all of Japan’s production needs, let alone broader allied needs.

    The disparity between China’s mining investments and those of the United States and its allies is most evident in Africa, home to some of the largest untapped mineral resources. Whereas the United States invested about $300 million in critical mineral projects on the continent in 2023, China invested about $8 billion to $10 billion. Washington has recognized the need to close this gap, but it still has a long way to go.

    Recent findings suggest that in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a particular focus of the Trump administration, Chinese companies control about 70 percent of cobalt and copper mines. Between 2008 and 2020, Chinese banks and companies extended over $9 billion in credit for mine development and operations in Congo, in addition to $3 billion in infrastructure loans from the Export-Import Bank of China. The United States and other G-7 countries had the opportunity to take part in these investments but judged the projects to be too risky. In 2015, for example, the Canadian-listed mining company Ivanhoe Mines sought funding for its Kamoa-Kakula copper project in Congo. With no Western investors willing to take on the risk, the Chinese firm Zijin Mining acquired an ownership stake. Today, Kamoa-Kakula is on track to become one of the largest copper mines in the world. Meanwhile, in 2016 and 2020, the only major American mining company active in Congo sold its stakes in two substantial copper-cobalt deposits, its only remaining stakes in the country, to a Chinese mining company.

    According to recent reports, the owners of a mine control where its minerals eventually go. When Chinese firms own a mine, the output flows either to their refineries or downstream manufacturers in China. The Chinese battery giant CATL, for example, has an ownership stake in the Kisanfu mine in Congo, where it secures a steady supply of copper and cobalt for its batteries. U.S. automakers and allied battery producers have also invested in some projects, but none to the same degree—even still, much of that material flows through China. The concentration of this refined material in China gives Beijing ever-greater market power and the ability to weaponize it.

    Industry observers note that in theory, the United States and its allies have the means of financing their own pipeline of future mining projects. In 2024, two Toronto-based stock exchanges hosted nearly 1,100 publicly listed mining companies, 40 percent of the global total. These companies account for roughly one-third of the world’s total mining equity capital raised over the last five years. About half of the listed companies’ projects were based in Canada. The Australian Stock Exchange is another key exchange, with about 850 companies listed in 2024 for mining development.

    Sources indicate that but these companies are facing pressures that discourage investment in promising projects. The world’s most accessible mineral deposits have already been tapped, so potential upcoming deposits are often located in more complicated geological environments, making the early stages of exploration more difficult and costly. Moving from exploration to production is also taking more time, as increased social and environmental requirements draw out permitting processes. This lengthening timeline lowers private investors’ appetite for risk because they have to wait longer for their investments to start generating returns. At the same time, Chinese overproduction of critical minerals has depressed prices for key commodities. Despite strong signals that demand for the minerals will continue to increase, these low prices discourage new players from entering the game and weaken investors’ incentives to help those already in it.

    U.S. and allied governments therefore need to draw in substantial new investment. The United States has made a start by taking equity stakes in domestic and international mining companies and expanding loans to them. Official announcements claim that these investments total around $50 billion, although the value of the deals that have been signed falls closer to $9 billion, and the money actually moving adds up to around $4 billion. Most of this money does not go to the projects languishing in the valley of death. Instead, the projects getting funded are those that are closer to production, because they can help tackle immediate supply risks.

    In a recent development, this is a good start, but ventures that remain at early stages still need funding, and private investors are still wary of mining projects. Since 2025, the few institutional investors that have gotten involved tended to do so after the U.S. government declared an equity stake or loan to back a project. Although such caution is not newly introduced, relying on government signals and public investment sets up a perverse incentive for private companies not to invest in the absence of public support, which is exactly what governments want to avoid.

    To really pull in private capital for exploration and mine development, the United States and the European Union should take a page from Canada’s book. The Canadian government offers tax credits to companies engaged in mineral exploration, and its “flow-through shares” system helps mining companies finance exploration and development by offering tax incentives to investors. If the rest of the G-7 can establish this kind of financial architecture, far more exploration capital would flow to critical mineral projects. And if member countries link their systems by letting investors claim tax benefits for exploration anywhere in the G-7, they could build the large, shared pool of exploration and development capital needed to support projects through to construction. In addition, G-7 countries must remove barriers for large institutional investors to enter the mining sector—primarily by reforming their tax codes, which at the moment disincentivize tax-exempt investors, such as pension funds, endowments, and foundations, from investing in mining projects because returns on such investments can be taxed as income.

    Finally, when the incentives for private investment still do not line up for certain projects, G-7 countries should use public capital to directly help mining companies escape the valley of death. To do this, the United States, Japan, and European countries should set up a joint facility to pool financing for feasibility studies, which are particularly difficult to raise private funding for, establishing a broad portfolio so that the losses from any failures are covered by the winners. This pooled fund would allocate grants to promising projects in exchange for equity in the project or a royalty once the mine goes into production. Many projects would still fail, but with a dedicated, well-staffed facility, the quality of investments would likely improve—as they have for China, which takes a similar portfolio approach to early-stage mining. And the benefits to both investors and national interests would far outweigh the lost capital.

    Industry observers note that today’s chokepoints for critical minerals sit mostly at the processing or refining stage, but future threats to the minerals needed for manufacturing, energy, artificial intelligence, and defense technology will be at the mines. G-7 countries have the markets and the policy tools to build a pipeline of secure mining projects and prevent the next economic emergency. Investment in refining facilities means little if the United States and its allies have no minerals to feed them a decade from now. The only choice, then, is to commit to financing new mining projects now.
